title: Linking predator–prey diel activity to predation patterns
content:
There is growing interest in understanding patterns of temporal overlap between predators and prey, but it remains unclear how overlap in activity translates into the timing and frequency of predation events. Here, we explore the factors that mediate these relationships, drawing on theory, examples, and an agent-based model. Photo of puma (Puma concolor) feeding on black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) kill in the Santa Cruz Mountains, California; by Sebastian Kennerknecht.


Abstract

Time is a key ecological resource, and the partitioning of time among species can stabilize ecological interactions, including predation. Over ecological and evolutionary time scales, predator–prey interactions shape the diel activity patterns of both actors, and in turn, predator and prey activity drive patterns of predation. Recent methodological advances have facilitated the quantification of fine-scale animal temporal activity patterns. In response, there is growing interest in understanding patterns of diel overlap among predators and prey, with the assumption that temporal overlap translates into interaction frequency. However, the degree to which predator–prey diel overlap is correlated with the timing of predation should vary with predator and prey traits and environmental context. Here, we discuss the factors that should mediate the relationship between diel activity overlap and predation, including mobility, predator hunting and sensory modes, prey anti-predator defences, and diel variation in habitat selection. To formalize and visualize our hypotheses, we present the results from a simple agent-based model that highlights the context dependency of the link between overlap and predation. We contend that a core assumption underlying the study of temporal predator–prey dynamics—that overlap in activity translates into predation timing and frequency—is largely untested. Further, our agent-based model highlights key contributors to the decoupling of timing overlap and predation frequency, including predator sensory mode, predator and prey mobility, and, importantly, the predilection of predators to hunt while stationary or to hunt stationary prey. We suggest that future efforts quantify not only temporal overlap but also the timing of predation events, guided by the hypotheses presented here, to better understand the role of diel activity in predator–prey interactions. These insights may also shed light on the ecological implications of altered activity and overlap patterns under human disturbance.
